column25: Ingot B, lowest of the tested ingots. Exceptionally well reported, and useful to the survey as a counter-example: it states everything the schema asks for, including the coupling refractive index, which almost nothing else does. Two of its own observations support the premise of this study directly. First, the authors report a 'geometry effect': for most ingots the plate-shaped samples give the highest light collection, so the same material yields different numbers depending on the shape cut from it. Second, light yield varies along a single crystal fibre (9,978 to 9,191 ph/MeV, and elsewhere a 4.3 %/cm gradient), so the number depends on where in the crystal the interaction happened. Dopant concentrations per ingot are not given (no at.%, mol%, wt% or ppm appears in the text). The authors note the absolute yield here (a few thousand to ~13,000 ph/MeV) is far below the ~50,000 ph/MeV of non-ultrafast GAGG:Ce, which is the deliberate trade-off of heavy Ce-Mg codoping for speed.

column18: absolute: single-photoelectron calibration, divided by QE and by a Geant4-simulated light collection efficiency
column25: Cryostat geometry, LCE 24 percent. PRIOR ART FOR PAPER 0'S METHOD. This paper already does what we proposed: it divides the measured photoelectron count by the PMT quantum efficiency AND by a light-collection efficiency obtained from a Geant4 optical simulation (version 10.6.p01, G4OpticalPhysics, UNIFIED surface model), to recover an intrinsic photon yield. LCE was 81 percent with the crystal coupled directly to the PMT window and 24 percent inside the optical cryostat. They quote a 5 percent relative uncertainty on the simulated LCE. That figure is the point of contact with this study: our own one-at-a-time scan of the optical inputs for NaI(Tl) -- refractive index, bulk absorption, emission band shape -- moves the light-collection efficiency by 42 percent across models consistent with the available measurements and 76 percent across what the literature actually uses. A 5 percent uncertainty on a simulated LCE is therefore hard to sustain unless the optical inputs are pinned down far better than they are for NaI, which is among the best-characterised scintillators there is. The same paper reports 50,300 +- 4,800 ph/MeV for the same crystal coupled directly to the PMT window (LCE 81 percent) -- two configurations, two numbers, 6 percent apart. An earlier independent study is cited at 33,900 ph/MeV at room temperature for this material, 57 percent below this work.

column18: absolute: measured photoelectrons divided by QE and by a Monte-Carlo light collection efficiency (MCRIM); cross-checked against a CaWO4 reference
column25: The cleanest quantitative demonstration of this project's premise that the survey has turned up. The SAME crystal, in the SAME setup, with a 0.05 mm gap held by wires, gives 14.3 +- 0.2 detected photons with the gap empty and 24.5 +- 0.4 with the gap filled with Cargille optical gel (n = 1.46) -- a 71 percent change from the optical coupling alone. The authors compute light collection efficiencies of 0.25 and 0.43 for the two cases and divide them out to recover one intrinsic yield. Unusually complete reporting: surfaces polished to a stated 50 nm roughness, measured transmittance 76 percent at the 540 nm emission peak (96 percent after correcting for multiple reflection, giving an absorption coefficient of 0.039 /cm), refractive index 2.01 cited, no reflector used, PMT quantum efficiency from the manufacturer. This is prior art for the correction protocol and a model of how to report it; note that the quoted total uncertainty is 16 percent, several times the 5 percent claimed for a simulated LCE in arXiv:2509.26416.
